rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi treats polytheism as the root of social disorder: it corrupts belief and morality, so messengers necessarily begin by calling people to worship God alone.
rows.anchor: the root of all anarchy in a society is polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers warn of both a worldly punishment for denying them and punishment on Judgment Day; contextual indications make Noah's warning here a worldly one.
rows.anchor: two types of punishments: one that visits them in this very world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning's wording reflects a punishment so severe that it uproots a nation and ends its existence as a people.
rows.anchor: such is its intensity that it uproots a whole nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi links Noah's warning to 26:135 and reads 26:138–139 as the people's response and the worldly punishment that followed.
rows.anchor: In verse 135 of S ūrah Shu‘arā’, the words ascribed to prophet Noah (sws) are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elders' reply means they accuse Noah of insulting their forefathers' religion by rejecting the deities they worshipped.
rows.anchor: he has humiliated the religion of his forefathers by denying the deities they have been worshipping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They consider Noah's threat implausible because their financial and living conditions seem much better than his and his followers'.
rows.anchor: whereas their financial and living conditions are far superior to him and his followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's answer conveys his concern, sympathy, and selfless invitation: despite their hostility, he endures harm for their benefit and fears their punishment.
rows.anchor: This reply from Noah (sws) reflects his utter concern and sympathy as well as the selfless nature of his invite.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheism brings no good: while it persists, it creates disorder across every sphere of individual and collective life.
rows.anchor: as long as it exists, disorder and disruption will continue to plague every sphere of individual and collective lives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unanswered question expresses sorrow; it implies that people who reflected and abandoned arrogance would have been grateful for a messenger sent from among themselves.
rows.anchor: No answer is given to the question raised in this verse. This is because the question is meant to express sorrow.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger from among the people is a favor: they know his character, he speaks their language, and he reflects their nature, unlike a stranger descending from heaven.
rows.anchor: He speaks the same language and his heart reflects their nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The details left implicit are an eloquent concealment; expressing anguish to people already committed to criticism would serve no purpose.
rows.anchor: All these details are concealed in this style and this concealment is in fact a requisite of eloquence at this instance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger warns in order to produce fear of God, which makes people deserving of mercy in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: the real purpose of a messenger’s warning is to produce God’s fear and it is this fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who demand a sign to witness punishment and want to see angels are instead inviting God's doom.
rows.anchor: those who demand a sign for punishment and want to observe angels only invite God’s doom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only those who persisted in denying Noah and God's signs were drowned.
rows.anchor: only those were drowned who persisted in his denial and in the denial of God’s signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice is to send decisive punishment only after a messenger has conclusively communicated the truth to a people.
rows.anchor: His punishment visits only those people to whom truth has been conclusively communicated by their respective messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's people inhabited the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
rows.anchor: Noah’s people inhabited the land between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether humans lived elsewhere then is speculative, so Islahi refrains from claiming either way.
rows.anchor: is a question whose answer is based on information that is speculative. So I would refrain from commenting on it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A disaster that serves as a trial can awaken a nation and affect both righteous and wrongdoers; it need not single out evildoers.
rows.anchor: These are God-sent in order to awaken it from its slumber.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike a trial, decisive torment follows conclusive communication and strikes the wrongdoers, while reformers and those following them are saved.
rows.anchor: In this case, only the wrongdoers are affected by it. Others who have taken up the task of reformation or are followers who take up this task are saved.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural ʿamūn derives from ʿamā, which can mean physical or intellectual blindness; here it means blindness of intellect.
rows.anchor: This word means those who are blind in the eye and can also mean those who are blind in their intellect. Here it is used in the latter meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people were destroyed because they had lost their intellect: a messenger is the final means of conclusive communication, and ignoring his warning negates their worldly existence.
rows.anchor: A messenger of God is the final means of conclusive communication of the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿĀd were Arabia's oldest nation, of Semitic descent, and lived in al-Aḥqāf.
rows.anchor: The ‘ Ād were the oldest nation of Arabia. They belonged to the Semitic race. Their abode was the land of A ḥqāf.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From the statement that God made them successors to Noah's people, Islahi infers that ʿĀd elders migrated north after the flood and gradually gained power and splendor.
rows.anchor: some elders of this nation migrated to the northern part of Arabia and gradually achieved great majesty and splendour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classical Arabic literature made the ʿĀd proverbial for height, bravery, and chivalry.
rows.anchor: In classical Arabic literature, they are proverbial for their height and also in their bravery and chivalry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Hūd their brother refers to the favor of a messenger from among them; such a favor was not valued by nations.
rows.anchor: The word “their brother” refers to God’s favour to the people of Hūd (sws) mentioned at other instances as “a messenger from among them.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd's question about whether they fear parallels Noah's earlier warning that he fears a terrible day for his people.
rows.anchor: The words “then do you not have fear” of H ūd (sws) occur in the same context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd's people saw prosperity as proof of God's favor and their right path; accordingly, they dismissed his messenger claim as a lie and foolishness.
rows.anchor: thought that their prosperity was not a means of earning wrath; it showed that they have favour in the eyes of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger's attribute amīn means trustworthy; a messenger must faithfully deliver the message entrusted to him, as in 26:143.
rows.anchor: A great trait of a messenger is that he us trustworthy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being made successors to Noah's people means political authority, not rule over the same land: Noah's people lived in the north and Hūd's in the south.
rows.anchor: The latter inhabited the north and the former lived in the south.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succession recalls God's favor but also warns ʿĀd through Noah's fate: the same divine law applies, so a similar attitude can bring a similar end.
rows.anchor: These words of Hūd (sws) not only recount God’s favour to his nation but also carry warning in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq means form, which can be internal or external; 4:119 illustrates distorting God's created form, as idolaters corrupted their natures and cut animals' ears.
rows.anchor: This form can refer to both internal and external forms.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basṭa and basṭatan both mean vastness or immensity, here denoting superiority in intellect and physique; Arab traditions support this, and 2:247 similarly describes Saul's knowledge and physique.
rows.anchor: It means “vastness” and “immensity.” Granting vastness in both internal and external forms means that they were given superiority in their intellect and in their physique.

rows.speaker: lexicographers
rows.claim: Lexicographers generally interpret ālāʾ as “favours.”
rows.anchor: Generally, lexicographers regard it to mean “favours.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects that gloss and says ālāʾ means feats, miracles, majesty, and splendor.
rows.anchor: However, this is not true. It means feats, miracles, majesty and splendour.

rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī
rows.claim: Al-Farāhī researched the word's sense in Mufradāt al-Qur’ān and cited ten pre-Qur'anic poetic couplets to support these meanings.
rows.anchor: My mentor, Ḥamīd al-D īn al-Far āhī, in his Mufradāt al-Qur’ ān has researched the meaning of this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd's reminder calls his people to value God's gifts of intellect and physique, be grateful, avoid arrogance, and remember God's majesty as the path to success, since His grasp is severe.
rows.anchor: What H ūd (sws) has said here encapsulates both favour and warning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's challenge to Hūd conveys both anger and sarcasm.
rows.anchor: Concealed in this sentence from his nation is both anger and sarcasm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They had expected Hūd to increase the standing of their ancestral religion and their own standing, yet he had become everyone's enemy.
rows.anchor: his people actually had high expectations from H ūd (sws) to further increase the respect of their ancestral religion and their own too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They say his threats will not awe them into abandoning their ancestral religion, even if his claim about God's punishment is true.
rows.anchor: they will not be over-awed by his threats and abandon their ancestral religion even if H ūd (sws) is truthful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd's phrasing resembles 16:1: the punishment is decreed and they have become worthy of it; only the time of its appearance remains.
rows.anchor: In other words, this thing has been destined to happen and they have become worthy of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijs literally means filth or impurity and here refers to disbelief, polytheism, and sinful conduct.
rows.anchor: means “filth” and “impurity.” Here it refers to the filth of disbelief and polytheism as well to misdeeds and bad conduct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the filth of disbelief and misconduct has an intrinsic cause-and-effect relation to God's wrath.
rows.anchor: There is an intrinsic relation of cause and effect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the people are demanding punishment, its manifestation is near.
rows.anchor: if the people of H ūd (sws)are demanding punishment, not much time is left
